entries.meaning: In a small, delicate, graceful way. ---
examples: She sipped her tea daintily.
The cat stepped daintily over the puddle.
He daintily dabbed his mouth with a napkin.

entries.meaning: Very; extremely (informal). ---
examples: That was a damn good meal.
You know damn well what I mean.
It's damn cold out there.
entries.modifies: adjectives and adverbs (damn good, damn well)
entries.form: flat — the same form as the adjective damn
entries.contrast: Informal and mildly offensive; keep it out of formal writing. Damn well adds force to a verb (You know damn well). Darn is the softer version.

entries.meaning: In a way that could cause harm or put someone at risk. ---
examples: He was driving dangerously fast.
The patient's blood pressure was dangerously low.
The crowd surged dangerously toward the stage.
entries.modifies: verbs, adjectives and adverbs (dangerously low, dangerously fast)

entries.meaning: Boldly; in a way that takes risks. ---
examples: The climber daringly scaled the cliff without ropes.
She dressed daringly for the gala.
The novel is daringly original.

entries.meaning: Darkly has 2 distinct senses.
examples: He hinted darkly at trouble ahead.
She muttered darkly about lawsuits.
The show is darkly funny.
The car had darkly tinted windows.
The hallway was darkly lit.

senses.head: In a gloomy, threatening, or mysterious way
examples: He hinted darkly at trouble ahead.
She muttered darkly about lawsuits.
The show is darkly funny.

senses.head: With a dark color or little light
examples: The car had darkly tinted windows.
The hallway was darkly lit.

entries.meaning: In a stylish, confident, attractive way. ---
examples: He looked dashingly handsome in his uniform.
The actor was dashingly dressed in a white suit.
The hero rode dashingly to the rescue.

entries.meaning: In a way that seems hard or big enough to discourage you. ---
examples: The reading list is dauntingly long.
The math behind the model is dauntingly complex.
Her calendar for the week looked dauntingly full.

entries.meaning: Every day for a long time, often tiresomely. ---
examples: He wore the same shirt day after day.
Day after day, she waited for a letter.
It rained day after day.
entries.русский: день за днём, изо дня в день
entries.contrast: Day after day stresses tiring repetition; day by day stresses gradual change. The day after tomorrow (послезавтра) is unrelated.

entries.meaning: Day by day has 2 distinct senses.
examples: Day by day, he's getting stronger.
Her English improved day by day.
Since the diagnosis, we take things day by day.
With no steady job, he's living day by day.

senses.head: Gradually, a little more each day
examples: Day by day, he's getting stronger.
Her English improved day by day.

senses.head: One day at a time, without planning far ahead
examples: Since the diagnosis, we take things day by day.
With no steady job, he's living day by day.

entries.meaning: Every day, continuously and without change, often to the point of boredom. ---
examples: She rides the same crowded train day in, day out.
Day in, day out, he answers the same customer complaints.
Farmers work the land day in, day out, whatever the weather.

entries.meaning: So brightly or impressively that it dazzles. ---
examples: The snow was dazzlingly bright.
She gave a dazzlingly good performance.
The lake sparkled dazzlingly in the sun.

entries.meaning: In fact or in practice, though not officially. ---
examples: English functions de facto as the official language of the United States.
After the governor fell ill, his chief of staff was de facto in charge.
The rule was never repealed, but it has been de facto abandoned.
entries.type: viewpoint — in actual practice, whatever the law says
entries.contrast: Much more often an adjective before a noun: the de facto leader, a de facto ban. Its legal opposite is de jure (по закону).

entries.meaning: Straight ahead; directly in front. ---
examples: There's a gas station dead ahead.
The captain spotted an iceberg dead ahead.
Keep driving and you'll see the lake dead ahead.

entries.meaning: Extremely; completely. ---
examples: I'm deadly serious about this.
The lecture was deadly dull.
The room went deadly quiet.
entries.modifies: a few adjectives: serious, dull, quiet, pale
entries.form: flat — the same form as the adjective deadly
entries.contrast: Usually an adjective (a deadly virus). As an adverb it only intensifies a few words: deadly serious means completely serious, not dangerously serious.

entries.meaning: Extremely, in a way that suggests death. ---
examples: She turned deathly pale.
The house was deathly quiet.
He was deathly afraid of snakes.
entries.modifies: a few adjectives: pale, quiet, still, afraid
entries.form: flat — the same form as the adjective deathly

entries.meaning: In a dishonest way meant to trick people. ---
examples: He deceitfully concealed his debts.
The company acted deceitfully toward its customers.
She was deceitfully lured into the scheme.

entries.meaning: Decently has 2 distinct senses.
examples: Treat people decently, whatever their job.
Please dress decently for the interview.
He behaved decently after the breakup.
The job pays decently.
She did decently on the exam.

senses.head: In a proper, respectable, or fair way
examples: Treat people decently, whatever their job.
Please dress decently for the interview.
He behaved decently after the breakup.

senses.head: Fairly well; well enough
examples: The job pays decently.
She did decently on the exam.

entries.meaning: In a way that gives a false impression. ---
examples: The puzzle looks deceptively simple.
The current is deceptively strong near the shore.
The drink was deceptively labeled as juice.
entries.contrast: Deceptively simple means it only looks simple and is really hard. With some adjectives the meaning is unclear (deceptively large — bigger or smaller than it looks?), so careful writers avoid those.

entries.meaning: Clearly; without doubt. ---
examples: The weather turned decidedly colder.
The mood in the room was decidedly hostile.
Her new album is decidedly better than the last one.
entries.contrast: Decidedly means clearly, definitely (decidedly colder). Decisively means firmly, without hesitating or by a clear margin (act decisively, win decisively).

entries.meaning: Decisively has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The governor acted decisively to stop the outbreak.
She answered decisively.
The home team won decisively.
Voters decisively rejected the measure.

senses.head: Quickly and firmly, without hesitating
examples: The governor acted decisively to stop the outbreak.
She answered decisively.

senses.head: In a way that settles something clearly
examples: The home team won decisively.
Voters decisively rejected the measure.

entries.meaning: In one's real feelings or nature, as opposed to how things seem. ---
examples: Deep down, I knew he was right.
She acts tough, but she's a kind person deep down.
Deep down, everyone wants to be liked.
entries.type: viewpoint — in one's true feelings, beneath the surface

entries.meaning: Defensively has 2 distinct senses.
examples: 'I was only trying to help,' he said defensively.
She crossed her arms defensively.
The team played well defensively.
Drive defensively on icy roads.

senses.head: In a way that reacts to criticism as if under attack
examples: 'I was only trying to help,' he said defensively.
She crossed her arms defensively.

senses.head: So as to protect against attack, as in sports, war or driving
examples: The team played well defensively.
Drive defensively on icy roads.

entries.meaning: With polite respect for someone's rank or opinion. ---
examples: The staff spoke deferentially to the senator.
He bowed his head deferentially.
Reporters treated the coach far too deferentially.

entries.meaning: In a way that openly refuses to obey or give in. ---
examples: She lifted her chin defiantly.
The protesters stayed defiantly in the square.
'I won't apologize,' he said defiantly.

entries.meaning: Quickly and skillfully. ---
examples: She deftly changed the subject.
The chef deftly flipped the omelet.
He handled the tough questions deftly.

entries.meaning: In a sad, discouraged way. ---
examples: He walked dejectedly off the field.
She sighed dejectedly and closed her laptop.
The fans sat dejectedly in the rain.

entries.meaning: Deliberately has 2 distinct senses.
examples: Someone set the fire deliberately.
She deliberately ignored my texts.
He deliberately left out the bad news.
He spoke slowly and deliberately.
She walked deliberately to the podium.

senses.head: On purpose
examples: Someone set the fire deliberately.
She deliberately ignored my texts.
He deliberately left out the bad news.

senses.head: Slowly and carefully
examples: He spoke slowly and deliberately.
She walked deliberately to the podium.

entries.comparison: more/most — mainly in the second sense

entries.meaning: Delicately has 2 distinct senses.
examples: She delicately raised the subject of money.
Handle the old photographs delicately.
The soup is delicately flavored with ginger.
The vase is delicately painted with birds.

senses.head: Carefully and tactfully, so as not to offend or damage anything
examples: She delicately raised the subject of money.
Handle the old photographs delicately.

senses.head: In a fine, light, or subtle way
examples: The soup is delicately flavored with ginger.
The vase is delicately painted with birds.

entries.meaning: Deliciously has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The pie smelled deliciously of cinnamon.
The sauce is deliciously rich.
The breeze was deliciously cool.
The ending is deliciously wicked.

senses.head: In a way that tastes or smells very good
examples: The pie smelled deliciously of cinnamon.
The sauce is deliciously rich.

senses.head: Very pleasantly; in a way that is great fun
examples: The breeze was deliciously cool.
The ending is deliciously wicked.

entries.meaning: With great pleasure. ---
examples: The kids squealed delightedly.
She clapped delightedly when she saw the cake.
He laughed delightedly at the joke.

entries.meaning: In a way that gives great pleasure. ---
examples: The hotel was delightfully quiet.
The film is delightfully weird.
She sang delightfully at the wedding.
entries.contrast: Delightfully describes what gives pleasure (a delightfully quiet hotel); delightedly describes a person who feels it (she clapped delightedly).

entries.meaning: Deliriously has 2 distinct senses.
examples: They were deliriously happy.
The crowd cheered deliriously.
He muttered deliriously through the night.
She talked deliriously while the fever lasted.

senses.head: Extremely, with wild excitement
examples: They were deliriously happy.
The crowd cheered deliriously.

senses.head: In a confused state caused by fever or illness
examples: He muttered deliriously through the night.
She talked deliriously while the fever lasted.

entries.meaning: By voting or in a way that gives everyone an equal say. ---
examples: The council was democratically elected.
The club makes its decisions democratically.
It was the country's first democratically chosen government.

entries.meaning: In a way that can be clearly shown or proved. ---
examples: The claim is demonstrably false.
The new drug is demonstrably safer.
Schools that tried it saw demonstrably better results.

entries.meaning: In a quiet, modest, reserved way. ---
examples: She smiled demurely and looked down.
The children sat demurely in the front pew.
She was demurely dressed in a long gray skirt.

entries.meaning: With parts or people crowded closely together. ---
examples: Manhattan is densely populated.
The hills are densely wooded.
The book is densely packed with footnotes.

entries.meaning: In a way you can rely on. ---
examples: The old truck still runs dependably.
She has dependably shown up early for ten years.
The furnace worked dependably all winter.

entries.meaning: In a shockingly bad way that deserves strong criticism. ---
examples: The refugees were treated deplorably.
The animals were kept in deplorably dirty cages.
Staffing at the hospital is deplorably low.

entries.meaning: In a way that makes you feel sad or hopeless. ---
examples: The results were depressingly familiar.
Depressingly, nothing has changed since then.
It rains depressingly often here.
entries.modifies: adjectives and adverbs; a whole clause at the front

entries.meaning: In a mocking way that shows contempt. ---
examples: The crowd laughed derisively.
Critics derisively called the stadium 'the money pit.'
He snorted derisively at the idea.

entries.meaning: As someone or something deserves; rightly. ---
examples: The film deservedly won best picture.
She is deservedly proud of her work.
The restaurant is popular, and deservedly so.
entries.modifies: verbs, adjectives, or a whole clause (and deservedly so)

entries.meaning: In a way that shows you have lost all hope. ---
examples: 'What do we do now?' she asked despairingly.
He shook his head despairingly.
They looked despairingly at the flooded basement.

entries.meaning: Desperately has 2 distinct senses.
examples: He fought desperately to stay afloat.
She searched desperately for a way out.
The town desperately needs a new hospital.
They were desperately poor.
I desperately wanted that job.

senses.head: With despair, trying anything because the situation is so bad
examples: He fought desperately to stay afloat.
She searched desperately for a way out.

senses.head: Extremely; very much
examples: The town desperately needs a new hospital.
They were desperately poor.
I desperately wanted that job.

entries.meaning: In a morally shameful way that deserves contempt. ---
examples: He behaved despicably toward his staff.
The scammers despicably targeted the elderly.
Treating a child that way is despicably cruel.

entries.meaning: In a sad, hopeless, discouraged way. ---
examples: He stared despondently at the rejection letter.
The players trudged despondently to the locker room.
She sat despondently by the phone.

entries.meaning: In a way that causes damage or harm. ---
examples: The storm moved destructively along the coast.
He handled his anger destructively.
Some teens use social media destructively.

entries.meaning: With firm purpose; refusing to give up. ---
examples: She worked determinedly toward her degree.
He determinedly ignored the pain.
The toddler marched determinedly toward the cookies.

entries.meaning: In a harmful way (formal). ---
examples: Stress can detrimentally affect your health.
The new rules may detrimentally impact small businesses.
Too much screen time can affect sleep detrimentally.

entries.meaning: In terms of a child's physical or mental growth. ---
examples: The toys are developmentally appropriate for toddlers.
Their son is developmentally delayed.
Developmentally, twins usually catch up by age two.

entries.meaning: Very; extremely. ---
examples: He was devilishly handsome.
The puzzle is devilishly hard.
It's a devilishly clever plot.

entries.meaning: In a sneaky, dishonest way. ---
examples: He deviously shifted the blame to his partner.
She smiled deviously as she dealt the cards.
The contract was deviously worded.

entries.meaning: With loyal love and care. ---
examples: She cared devotedly for her mother.
The dog followed him devotedly.
Fans have devotedly watched the show for twenty years.

entries.meaning: Devoutly has 2 distinct senses.
examples: Her family is devoutly Catholic.
He prayed devoutly every morning.
I devoutly hope this is the last meeting.
It's an outcome we should all devoutly wish for.

senses.head: In a deeply religious way
examples: Her family is devoutly Catholic.
He prayed devoutly every morning.

senses.head: Sincerely; very much, with hope or wish
examples: I devoutly hope this is the last meeting.
It's an outcome we should all devoutly wish for.

entries.modifies: verbs and adjectives (devoutly Catholic, devoutly hope)

entries.meaning: With skillful use of the hands or mind. ---
examples: The surgeon dexterously tied the stitches.
He shuffled the cards dexterously.
She dexterously avoided the reporter's question.

entries.meaning: In an extremely wicked or fiendishly clever way. ---
examples: The plan was diabolically clever.
The final exam was diabolically hard.
The villain laughed diabolically.

entries.meaning: In a slanting line from one corner to the opposite one. ---
examples: Cut the bread diagonally.
We walked diagonally across the park.
The bank is diagonally across from the post office.
entries.modifies: verbs of movement and cutting; across

entries.meaning: Completely, as far apart as possible. ---
examples: Their views are diametrically opposed.
The two plans go in diametrically opposite directions.
She and her father hold diametrically opposed opinions.

entries.meaning: In another way; not in the same way. ---
examples: Everyone learns differently.
She sees things differently now.
I would have done it differently.
entries.contrast: Standard English uses differently after a verb; think different is a slogan, not correct grammar. Americans usually say differently than (she acts differently than her sister); differently from is also correct.

entries.meaning: Shyly, without confidence. ---
examples: He diffidently offered his opinion.
She knocked diffidently on the office door.
'Maybe we could try again?' he asked diffidently.

entries.meaning: By means of computers or digital technology. ---
examples: The photos were digitally altered.
You can sign the form digitally.
The old films have been digitally restored.

entries.meaning: With steady, careful effort. ---
examples: She studied diligently for the bar exam.
Crews worked diligently to restore power.
He diligently checked every receipt.

entries.meaning: Dimly has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The bar was dimly lit.
A lamp glowed dimly in the window.
I dimly remember the house we lived in.
She was dimly aware of someone calling her name.

senses.head: With little light
examples: The bar was dimly lit.
A lamp glowed dimly in the window.

senses.head: Vaguely; not clearly
examples: I dimly remember the house we lived in.
She was dimly aware of someone calling her name.

entries.position: before its word; also mid or end
entries.modifies: participles, adjectives and verbs (dimly lit, dimly aware)

entries.meaning: Diplomatically has 2 distinct senses.
examples: She diplomatically suggested a shorter speech.
He answered the question diplomatically.
The border dispute was resolved diplomatically.
The country is diplomatically isolated.

senses.head: Tactfully, so as not to upset anyone
examples: She diplomatically suggested a shorter speech.
He answered the question diplomatically.

senses.head: Through diplomacy between countries
examples: The border dispute was resolved diplomatically.
The country is diplomatically isolated.

entries.meaning: In an unpleasant or bad-tempered way. ---
examples: The room was disagreeably hot.
He laughed disagreeably at her question.
The basement smelled disagreeably of mold.

entries.meaning: In a way that shows you feel let down. ---
examples: The kids groaned disappointedly.
She looked disappointedly at her score.
'Oh, that's all?' he said disappointedly.

entries.meaning: In a way that falls short of what was hoped for. ---
examples: Sales were disappointingly low.
Disappointingly, the museum was closed.
The sequel was disappointingly short.
entries.modifies: adjectives and adverbs; a whole clause at the front
entries.contrast: Disappointingly describes the thing that lets you down (disappointingly slow); disappointedly describes how a person feels (she sighed disappointedly).

entries.meaning: In a way that shows you think something is wrong or bad. ---
examples: She shook her head disapprovingly.
The librarian looked disapprovingly over her glasses.
He clicked his tongue disapprovingly.

entries.meaning: In a way that causes a disaster or turns out very badly. ---
examples: The launch went disastrously wrong.
The plan backfired disastrously.
The team played disastrously in the second half.

entries.meaning: In a way that shows you cannot believe something. ---
examples: She stared disbelievingly at the lottery ticket.
He laughed disbelievingly.
'You finished it already?' she asked disbelievingly.

entries.meaning: In a way that makes you uneasy or confused. ---
examples: The doctor was disconcertingly quiet.
The robot looks disconcertingly human.
Disconcertingly, no one answered the door.
entries.modifies: adjectives; a whole clause at the front

entries.meaning: Very sadly, in a way nothing can comfort. ---
examples: The boy sat disconsolately on the curb.
She wandered disconsolately through the empty house.
The fans stared disconsolately at the scoreboard.

entries.meaning: In a way that makes you lose hope or confidence. ---
examples: Progress has been discouragingly slow.
The early test results were discouragingly bad.
Discouragingly, only six people signed up.
entries.modifies: adjectives and adverbs; a whole clause at the front

entries.meaning: Quietly and carefully, so as not to attract attention or cause embarrassment. ---
examples: She discreetly slipped him a note.
The matter was handled discreetly.
He coughed discreetly to get their attention.
entries.contrast: Sounds exactly like discretely (separately, as distinct parts), a different and much rarer word.

entries.meaning: In a way that shows you think something is not worth your respect. ---
examples: She looked disdainfully at the cheap wine.
He disdainfully waved the offer away.
The critic wrote disdainfully about pop music.

entries.meaning: In a shamefully bad way. ---
examples: The fans behaved disgracefully.
The veterans were treated disgracefully.
The streets are disgracefully dirty.

entries.meaning: In a way that shows strong dislike or disgust. ---
examples: She wrinkled her nose disgustedly.
He tossed the moldy bread away disgustedly.
'That's gross,' the boy said disgustedly.

entries.meaning: Disgustingly has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The bathroom was disgustingly filthy.
He chewed disgustingly with his mouth open.
They're disgustingly rich.
She's always disgustingly cheerful in the morning.

senses.head: In a way that causes disgust
examples: The bathroom was disgustingly filthy.
He chewed disgustingly with his mouth open.

senses.head: To an annoying or enviable degree (informal, often joking)
examples: They're disgustingly rich.
She's always disgustingly cheerful in the morning.

entries.contrast: Disgustingly describes the thing that disgusts (disgustingly dirty); disgustedly describes how a person reacts (she said disgustedly).

entries.meaning: In a way that lies, cheats, or deceives. ---
examples: He obtained the money dishonestly.
The ad dishonestly suggests the pills cure cancer.
She admitted she had acted dishonestly.

entries.meaning: In a way that brings shame or breaks a moral code. ---
examples: He was dishonorably discharged from the Army.
They acted dishonorably in breaking the deal.
She refused to win dishonorably.
entries.contrast: US spelling. British English writes dishonourably.

entries.meaning: Insincerely, pretending to be innocent or to know less than you do. ---
examples: He disingenuously claimed he'd never seen the memo.
The company disingenuously called the layoffs a 'restructuring.'
She asked, a little disingenuously, what all the fuss was about.

entries.meaning: In a way that fails to support, or betrays, a friend, employer or country. ---
examples: He was fired for acting disloyally toward the company.
She felt her brother had behaved disloyally by taking their father's side.
Nobody on the team wanted to be caught speaking disloyally about the coach.
entries.modifies: verbs such as act, behave, speak

entries.meaning: Dismally has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The plan failed dismally.
Turnout was dismally low this year.
Our team played dismally in the second half.
"It's raining again," he said dismally.
She stared dismally at the pile of bills.

senses.head: Very badly; in a way that is a complete failure
examples: The plan failed dismally.
Turnout was dismally low this year.
Our team played dismally in the second half.

senses.head: In a gloomy, unhappy way
examples: "It's raining again," he said dismally.
She stared dismally at the pile of bills.

entries.position: end — after the verb, most often fail; before its word with adjectives (dismally low)

entries.meaning: In a way that shows you think someone or something has little value or importance. ---
examples: He spoke disparagingly of his former boss.
Critics wrote disparagingly about the remake.
She referred disparagingly to the plan as a "wish list."
entries.position: end — usually after speak, talk or write, before of or about

entries.meaning: Calmly and fairly, without letting personal feelings take over. ---
examples: A judge has to weigh the evidence dispassionately.
She described the accident dispassionately, as if it had happened to someone else.
Try to look at the numbers dispassionately.
entries.position: end — after the verb or its object
entries.modifies: verbs such as look at, consider, describe

entries.meaning: Much more or much less than is fair or expected compared with others. ---
examples: Low-income families are disproportionately affected by the tax.
Rents have risen disproportionately in the city center.
The company spends disproportionately on marketing.
entries.position: before its word — before a participle or adjective (disproportionately affected); end after a verb

entries.meaning: Rudely, without showing proper respect. ---
examples: He was suspended for speaking disrespectfully to a teacher.
Please don't talk about your grandmother so disrespectfully.
A few fans behaved disrespectfully during the national anthem.

entries.meaning: In a way that interrupts or disturbs what other people are doing. ---
examples: Students who behave disruptively will be asked to leave.
A phone rang disruptively in the middle of the ceremony.
The protesters acted disruptively but peacefully.

entries.meaning: Distantly has 2 distinct senses.
examples: We're distantly related through my mother's side.
A dog barked distantly somewhere across the field.
She smiled distantly and kept walking.
He answered distantly, clearly thinking about something else.

senses.head: Far away, or not closely connected
examples: We're distantly related through my mother's side.
A dog barked distantly somewhere across the field.

senses.head: In a cool, unfriendly way that keeps people at a distance
examples: She smiled distantly and kept walking.
He answered distantly, clearly thinking about something else.

entries.position: end — after verbs like smile and answer; before its word in distantly related
entries.modifies: related and similar adjectives; verbs like smile, hear, answer

entries.meaning: In a way that is typical of one person, place or thing and makes it easy to recognize. ---
examples: The song has a distinctively Southern sound.
Her handwriting is distinctively round and neat.
The coffee has a distinctively smoky flavor.
entries.position: before its word — before an adjective or participle (distinctively American); end after a verb
entries.contrast: Do not confuse with distinctly 'clearly, noticeably': a distinctly cold room is noticeably cold, while a distinctively designed room has its own recognizable style.

entries.meaning: Distinctly has 2 distinct senses.
examples: I distinctly remember locking the door.
Speak slowly and distinctly into the microphone.
I distinctly heard her say no.
The room felt distinctly colder after sunset.
His tone was distinctly unfriendly.

senses.head: Clearly, so that it is easy to hear, see or remember
examples: I distinctly remember locking the door.
Speak slowly and distinctly into the microphone.
I distinctly heard her say no.

senses.head: Noticeably; definitely
examples: The room felt distinctly colder after sunset.
His tone was distinctly unfriendly.

entries.position: mid or end — with remember, hear, say; before its word with adjectives (distinctly odd)
entries.modifies: verbs of perceiving, speaking and remembering; adjectives
entries.contrast: Not the same as distinctively 'in a characteristic, recognizable way' — see that entry.

entries.meaning: Without paying full attention, because you are thinking about something else. ---
examples: He nodded distractedly while scrolling through his phone.
She distractedly stirred her coffee.
"Sure, sure," he said distractedly.

entries.meaning: To a degree that is upsetting or worrying. ---
examples: The error rate remains distressingly high.
Cases like this are distressingly common.
Distressingly, nobody called the police.
entries.position: before its word — before an adjective; front as a comment on the whole sentence

entries.meaning: In a way or to a degree that is worrying or upsetting. ---
examples: The movie is disturbingly realistic.
The number of overdoses has risen disturbingly fast.
Disturbingly, the files were left on an open server.
entries.position: before its word — before an adjective or adverb; front as a comment on the whole sentence
entries.modifies: adjectives, adverbs, or a whole sentence

entries.meaning: By God or a god; as an act of heaven. ---
examples: Many believers see the text as divinely inspired.
Kings once claimed they were divinely appointed to rule.
She felt her recovery had been divinely guided.
entries.position: before its word — before a participle (divinely inspired)
entries.modifies: participles such as inspired, ordained, appointed

entries.meaning: In an unsteady way, with a spinning feeling in your head. ---
examples: He stood up too fast and swayed dizzily.
The room spun dizzily around her.
The kids staggered dizzily off the merry-go-round.
entries.form: -ly from dizzy, with y becoming i
entries.contrast: Dizzily describes how someone who feels dizzy moves, or how things spin around them. For something that makes you dizzy, like a height or a pace, Americans say dizzyingly: dizzyingly high, not dizzily high.

entries.meaning: With stubborn determination, refusing to give up. ---
examples: She doggedly pursued the story for two years.
The team fought doggedly until the final whistle.
He worked doggedly through the pile of paperwork.
entries.modifies: verbs of effort such as pursue, fight, work
entries.form: -ly from dogged 'stubbornly determined', said in two syllables

entries.meaning: In a way that insists your beliefs are right and refuses to consider other views. ---
examples: He dogmatically refused to consider any other diet.
Don't apply the rules too dogmatically.
She argued dogmatically that there was only one right answer.
entries.modifies: verbs of saying, believing and applying rules

entries.meaning: Inside a country, as opposed to abroad. ---
examples: Most of the cars are sold domestically.
The airline flies domestically and to Canada.
We only buy domestically grown produce.
entries.position: end — after the verb or its object; before its word with participles (domestically produced)
entries.contrast: Russian домашний 'home' can mislead: domestically almost always means 'inside the country' — domestically produced means made in this country, not made at home.

entries.meaning: Double has 2 distinct senses.
examples: Taxis charge double after midnight.
Workers get paid double on holidays.
I had to pay double for a last-minute ticket.
After the hit to the head, he was seeing double.
Fold the sheet double before you cut it.
She was bent double with laughter.

senses.head: Twice as much; at twice the usual amount
examples: Taxis charge double after midnight.
Workers get paid double on holidays.
I had to pay double for a last-minute ticket.

senses.head: In two, or so that one thing looks like two
examples: After the hit to the head, he was seeing double.
Fold the sheet double before you cut it.
She was bent double with laughter.

entries.position: end — after the verb or its object
entries.modifies: verbs such as pay, charge, see, fold, bend
entries.form: flat — the same form as the adjective double
entries.contrast: After a verb the adverb stays flat: pay double, not pay doubly. Doubly goes before an adjective and means 'twice as': doubly important.

entries.meaning: Twice as much; for two reasons or in two ways. ---
examples: After the break-in, we were doubly careful to lock the door.
It's doubly important to drink water in this heat.
The loss was doubly painful because it came at home.
entries.position: before its word — before an adjective or participle

entries.meaning: In a way that shows you are not sure or do not quite believe something. ---
examples: She looked doubtfully at the old ladder.
"I guess it could work," he said doubtfully.
The customer eyed the price tag doubtfully.

entries.meaning: Toward the opponent's end of a sports field. ---
examples: The quarterback threw the ball downfield.
He broke a tackle and raced downfield.
She passed the ball downfield to an open teammate.
entries.position: end — after the verb or its object
entries.modifies: verbs of moving, throwing and kicking

entries.meaning: Completely; used to stress that something is bad or surprising. ---
examples: The service was slow and downright rude.
Some of the comments were downright offensive.
Driving in that snow was downright dangerous.
entries.position: before its word — before an adjective (downright rude)

entries.meaning: In the direction a river flows; farther along the river toward its mouth. ---
examples: We floated downriver on inner tubes.
The town is about ten miles downriver.
The logs were carried downriver to the mill.
entries.position: end — after a verb of motion or position

entries.meaning: Toward the front of a stage, nearer the audience. ---
examples: The actor walked downstage and spoke straight to the audience.
Take two steps downstage so the light catches your face.
The piano sits downstage left.
entries.position: end — after a verb of motion or position
entries.contrast: Downstage is toward the audience, not lower down; upstage is away from the audience. Stage left and right are also given from the actor's point of view.

entries.meaning: In the direction the wind is blowing. ---
examples: The smoke drifted downwind toward the highway.
Hunters try to stay downwind of the deer.
People living downwind of the plant complained about the smell.
entries.position: end — after a verb of motion or position, often with of
entries.modifies: verbs of motion and position (downwind of the fire)

entries.meaning: Dramatically has 2 distinct senses.
examples: Prices have risen dramatically since spring.
Crime dropped dramatically after the new lights went in.
The weather changed dramatically overnight.
She sighed dramatically and left the room.
He paused dramatically before the last line.

senses.head: By a large amount, often suddenly
examples: Prices have risen dramatically since spring.
Crime dropped dramatically after the new lights went in.
The weather changed dramatically overnight.

senses.head: In a theatrical, attention-seeking way
examples: She sighed dramatically and left the room.
He paused dramatically before the last line.

entries.position: mid or end — rose dramatically, dramatically improved
entries.contrast: A false friend: Russian драматически suggests tragedy, but English dramatically usually just means by a lot — sales rose dramatically is good news. Compare drastically, which implies a severe and often unwelcome change.

entries.meaning: In an extreme way that has a large and serious effect. ---
examples: The company drastically cut its travel budget.
Rents have gone up drastically in this neighborhood.
Things could have gone drastically wrong.
entries.position: mid or end — drastically cut, changed drastically
entries.contrast: Stronger and more negative than dramatically: drastically suggests harsh measures or a change for the worse (drastically reduced staff), while dramatically is neutral about whether the change is good.

entries.meaning: Dreadfully has 2 distinct senses.
examples: I'm dreadfully sorry for the mix-up.
It's dreadfully hot in here.
The house felt dreadfully empty after the kids left.
The actors performed dreadfully.
He treated his staff dreadfully.

senses.head: Very; extremely (a little old-fashioned)
examples: I'm dreadfully sorry for the mix-up.
It's dreadfully hot in here.
The house felt dreadfully empty after the kids left.

senses.head: Very badly
examples: The actors performed dreadfully.
He treated his staff dreadfully.

entries.position: before its word — before an adjective (dreadfully sorry); end after a verb in the 'badly' sense

entries.meaning: In a way that shows your mind is on pleasant thoughts rather than on what is around you. ---
examples: She gazed dreamily out the window.
"I'd love to live by the ocean," he said dreamily.
The kids sighed dreamily at the thought of summer.
entries.modifies: verbs such as smile, gaze, sigh, say

entries.meaning: Extremely, in dripping wet: so wet that water runs off. ---
examples: We came in from the storm dripping wet.
The dog climbed out of the lake dripping wet and shook itself.
Her hair was still dripping wet from the shower.
entries.form: the -ing form of drip, used as an intensifier
entries.contrast: Only dripping wet is adverbial. In a dripping faucet it is a participle, and in He was dripping with sweat it is the verb.

entries.meaning: Extremely; used informally to praise how someone or something looks. ---
examples: She looked drop-dead gorgeous in that dress.
The view from the terrace is drop-dead beautiful.
Her new boyfriend is drop-dead handsome.
entries.position: before its word — only before a few adjectives, mainly gorgeous
entries.modifies: a few adjectives of looks: gorgeous, beautiful, handsome
entries.form: compound of drop + dead — 'so striking you could drop dead'

entries.meaning: In a sleepy, half-awake way. ---
examples: He blinked drowsily at the alarm clock.
"What time is it?" she asked drowsily.
The cat stretched drowsily in the sun.

entries.meaning: In the way a drunk person behaves. ---
examples: Two fans were singing drunkenly outside the bar.
He stumbled drunkenly up the stairs.
She drunkenly insisted that she could drive.

entries.meaning: In a flat, unemotional way that hides humor or sarcasm. ---
examples: "Well, that went well," she said dryly.
He dryly noted that the meeting could have been an email.
The report dryly lists the company's many failures.
entries.position: end — after a verb of speaking; mid before the verb
entries.contrast: American spelling prefers dryly; drily is more common in British writing. Russian сухо often means 'coldly'; English dryly usually signals deadpan humor or sarcasm.

entries.meaning: Dubiously has 2 distinct senses.
examples: She looked dubiously at the gray meat.
"You fixed it yourself?" he asked dubiously.
The money was dubiously obtained.
The pills are dubiously marketed as a cure for anxiety.

senses.head: With doubt or suspicion
examples: She looked dubiously at the gray meat.
"You fixed it yourself?" he asked dubiously.

senses.head: In a way that is questionable or probably dishonest
examples: The money was dubiously obtained.
The pills are dubiously marketed as a cure for anxiety.

entries.position: end — after the verb; before its word with participles (dubiously obtained)
entries.modifies: verbs of saying and looking; participles

entries.meaning: Exactly in the direction of a compass point. ---
examples: The trail runs due north from the lake.
Sail due west for about two miles.
The storm is moving due east.
entries.position: before its word — before north, south, east or west
entries.form: flat — the same form as the adjective due
entries.contrast: Only before a compass point. Due in The rent is due is an adjective, and due to (due to the rain) works as a preposition — both belong to other dictionaries.

entries.meaning: Dully has 2 distinct senses.
examples: My knee ached dully all afternoon.
The old coins gleamed dully in the case.
The door thudded dully behind him.
He stared dully at the TV.
She answered dully, as if she hadn't slept.

senses.head: Not sharply or brightly: with a low sound, a weak light, or a steady ache
examples: My knee ached dully all afternoon.
The old coins gleamed dully in the case.
The door thudded dully behind him.

senses.head: Without interest or energy
examples: He stared dully at the TV.
She answered dully, as if she hadn't slept.

entries.meaning: In the proper or expected way; as required. ---
examples: The forms were duly signed and returned.
He is a duly elected member of the board.
I asked for a refund, and it duly arrived a week later.
entries.position: mid — before the main verb or the past participle
entries.modifies: verbs, often in the passive, and participles (duly elected)
entries.form: from due, dropping the e — not duely

entries.meaning: Silently, because you are too shocked, confused or upset to speak. ---
examples: She nodded dumbly, unable to find the words.
We stared dumbly at the wreckage.
He stood there dumbly while they read the verdict.
entries.modifies: verbs such as stare, nod, stand
entries.contrast: In American English dumb usually means 'stupid', so dumbly can also sound like 'stupidly'. The 'speechless' meaning survives mainly with stare, nod and stand.

entries.meaning: Because it is expected of you, not because you really want to. ---
examples: The kids dutifully wrote thank-you notes.
Reporters dutifully copied down every number.
He laughed dutifully at his boss's jokes.

entries.meaning: In a way that keeps changing and adjusting as things happen, or with a lot of energy. ---
examples: The page is generated dynamically from the database.
Prices change dynamically based on demand.
The city is growing dynamically.

entries.meaning: For example; used in writing before one or more examples. ---
examples: Bring something warm to wear (e.g., a jacket or sweater).
Avoid sugary drinks, e.g., soda and sports drinks.
Some fruits, e.g., bananas and avocados, keep ripening after they're picked.
entries.position: before its word — directly before the examples, usually after a comma or inside parentheses
entries.form: abbreviation of Latin exempli gratia 'for the sake of example'
entries.contrast: E.g. gives examples from a larger group; i.e. 'that is' restates exactly: citrus fruit, e.g., lemons but the capital, i.e., Moscow. American style puts a comma after both. In speech say for example.

entries.meaning: For, to or from every one of a group; apiece. ---
examples: The tickets are twenty dollars each.
The kids got two cookies each.
The two teams scored three goals each.
entries.position: after its word — after an amount (twenty dollars each)
entries.contrast: Russian puts по before the number (по двадцать долларов); English puts each after it: twenty dollars each, never each twenty dollars. Each before a noun (each ticket) is a determiner, covered in that dictionary.

entries.meaning: With strong interest, wanting very much to do or have something. ---
examples: The eagerly awaited sequel comes out Friday.
The kids ran eagerly to the door.
She eagerly agreed to help.

entries.meaning: At an early stage of something. ---
examples: I realized early on that the job wasn't for me.
Early on, the company had only three employees.
Problems like this are easier to fix if you catch them early on.

entries.meaning: Seriously and sincerely, with strong feeling. ---
examples: He spoke earnestly about the need for change.
I earnestly hope you'll reconsider.
She looked at me earnestly and asked for the truth.
entries.modifies: verbs of speaking, hoping and asking

entries.meaning: Easily has 3 distinct senses.
examples: She passed the test easily.
This recipe can easily be doubled.
I don't get lost easily.
It was easily the best meal of the trip.
The crowd was easily ten thousand people.
That could easily happen to anyone.
The trip could easily take longer than we planned.

senses.head: Without difficulty
examples: She passed the test easily.
This recipe can easily be doubled.
I don't get lost easily.

senses.head: Without any doubt; by far
examples: It was easily the best meal of the trip.
The crowd was easily ten thousand people.

senses.head: Very possibly; quite likely
examples: That could easily happen to anyone.
The trip could easily take longer than we planned.

entries.type: manner; also degree (easily the best) and stance (could easily happen)
entries.position: end — after the verb or its object; before its word before a superlative or a number; mid after a modal (could easily)
entries.modifies: verbs, superlatives, numbers, and modal verbs
entries.form: -ly from easy, with y becoming i
entries.contrast: Informal American speech keeps flat easy in set phrases — take it easy, go easy on him, easier said than done — but after most verbs the adverb is easily: She won easily, not She won easy.

entries.meaning: Toward or in the east. ---
examples: We drove east for three hours.
The house faces east, so we get the morning sun.
The town is twenty miles east of Denver.
entries.position: end — after a verb of motion or position
entries.form: flat — the same form as the noun and adjective east
entries.contrast: No preposition before the adverb: head east, not head to east. With the it is a noun: in the east, to the east of the city.

entries.meaning: In an unusual, odd way that is different from what most people do. ---
examples: He was eccentrically dressed in a cape and a top hat.
The old professor behaved eccentrically but was always kind.
The house was decorated eccentrically, with clocks on every wall.
entries.position: end — after the verb; before its word with participles (eccentrically dressed)

entries.meaning: In terms of the environment and how living things depend on it. ---
examples: The wetlands are ecologically important for migrating birds.
Is this farming method ecologically sustainable?
Ecologically, the dam was a disaster.
entries.position: before its word — before an adjective (ecologically sound); front as a comment
entries.contrast: Russian экологически чистый is usually environmentally friendly or eco-friendly in English, not ecologically clean.

entries.meaning: With great joy and excitement. ---
examples: The crowd cheered ecstatically when the winning run scored.
She hugged him ecstatically.
They were ecstatically happy with the new baby.
entries.position: end — after the verb; before its word with happy
entries.modifies: verbs, and adjectives such as happy

entries.meaning: Edgewise has 2 distinct senses.
examples: My aunt talked so much that I couldn't get a word in edgewise.
Let someone else get a word in edgewise for once.
We had to carry the table in edgewise.
Turn the board edgewise to get it through the door.

senses.head: Used in get a word in edgewise: to manage to say something while someone else talks nonstop
examples: My aunt talked so much that I couldn't get a word in edgewise.
Let someone else get a word in edgewise for once.

senses.head: With the edge first; sideways
examples: We had to carry the table in edgewise.
Turn the board edgewise to get it through the door.

entries.position: end — after the verb or its object
entries.modifies: get a word in, and verbs of moving and turning
entries.contrast: American English says edgewise; British English says edgeways.

entries.meaning: In terms of editing, or of a newspaper's official opinion. ---
examples: The magazine is editorially independent of its owners.
The paper argued editorially against the new stadium.
Editorially, the book still needs a lot of work.
entries.русский: с редакционной точки зрения; в редакционной статье
entries.position: before its word — before an adjective (editorially independent); end after a verb; front as a comment

entries.meaning: In terms of education or learning. ---
examples: The trip was fun and educationally valuable.
The program helps educationally disadvantaged children.
Educationally, the move was good for the kids.
entries.position: before its word — before an adjective; front as a comment

entries.meaning: In a strange, slightly frightening way. ---
examples: The streets were eerily quiet after the storm.
The two photos are eerily similar.
The wind howled eerily through the trees.
entries.position: before its word — before an adjective (eerily quiet); end after a verb
entries.form: -ly from eerie, with the final e becoming i

entries.meaning: Effectively has 2 distinct senses.
examples: She manages her time very effectively.
We need to communicate more effectively with customers.
The decision effectively ends his career.
With two minutes left, the game was effectively over.
The road is effectively closed until spring.

senses.head: In a way that works well and gets the result you want
examples: She manages her time very effectively.
We need to communicate more effectively with customers.

senses.head: In fact, even if not officially; virtually
examples: The decision effectively ends his career.
With two minutes left, the game was effectively over.
The road is effectively closed until spring.

entries.position: end — after the verb or its object in the 'well' sense; mid or before its word in the 'in fact' sense
entries.contrast: Russian эффективно covers only the first sense. In The company was effectively bankrupt, effectively means 'in reality, though not officially' — фактически, not эффективно.

entries.meaning: Well and quickly, without wasting time, money or energy. ---
examples: The new engine uses fuel more efficiently.
The staff worked quickly and efficiently.
We need to run the office more efficiently.
entries.position: end — after the verb or its object
entries.contrast: Efficiently is about not wasting time, money or energy; effectively is about getting the result. Russian эффективно is used for both.

entries.meaning: Easily, so that something hard looks as if it takes no effort. ---
examples: She switched effortlessly between English and Spanish.
The dancers moved effortlessly across the stage.
He effortlessly lifted the box onto the top shelf.

entries.meaning: With a lot of warm, emotional words, sometimes more than seems sincere. ---
examples: She thanked us effusively for the flowers.
Critics praised the film effusively.
He apologized effusively for being late.
entries.position: end — after the verb or its object
entries.modifies: verbs such as thank, praise, apologize

entries.meaning: With a lot of careful detail. ---
examples: The cake was elaborately decorated with sugar flowers.
They planned the surprise party elaborately.
The dancers wore elaborately embroidered costumes.
entries.position: before its word — before a participle (elaborately decorated); end after a verb

entries.meaning: By means of electricity, or in terms of electricity. ---
examples: The gates are electrically operated.
Most of the trains are electrically powered.
The wires must be electrically insulated.
entries.position: before its word — before a participle (electrically powered); end after a verb

entries.meaning: By computer or other electronic means. ---
examples: You can file your taxes electronically.
The documents were signed electronically.
Payments are sent electronically every two weeks.
entries.position: end — after the verb or its object

entries.meaning: In a stylish, graceful way; also, in a clever and simple way. ---
examples: She was elegantly dressed in black.
The room is elegantly furnished.
The new design solves the problem elegantly.
entries.position: end — after the verb; before its word with participles (elegantly dressed)

entries.meaning: In a clear, powerful and moving way, especially in speech or writing. ---
examples: She spoke eloquently about her years as a nurse.
The photos show the cost of war more eloquently than any speech.
He argued his case eloquently.
entries.position: end — after the verb or its object
entries.modifies: verbs of speaking, writing and showing

entries.meaning: To a degree that makes you feel awkward or ashamed. ---
examples: The answer was embarrassingly simple.
We lost by an embarrassingly wide margin.
Embarrassingly, I had forgotten her name.
entries.position: before its word — before an adjective; front as a comment on the whole sentence

entries.meaning: Very; used to stress a good quality. ---
examples: She is eminently qualified for the job.
That seems like an eminently reasonable request.
The book is eminently readable.
entries.position: before its word — before an adjective
entries.contrast: Do not confuse with imminently 'very soon, about to happen': eminently qualified, but a storm is imminent.

entries.meaning: In a way that shows you understand how someone else feels. ---
examples: The nurse listened empathetically as he described the pain.
She nodded empathetically.
Good managers respond empathetically when employees struggle.
entries.modifies: verbs such as listen, respond, nod

entries.meaning: Strongly and clearly, leaving no doubt. ---
examples: The mayor emphatically denied the rumors.
"No," she said emphatically.
This is emphatically not the time to quit.
entries.position: mid or end; before its word before not (emphatically not)
entries.modifies: verbs of saying, not, and adjectives

entries.meaning: By observation and experiment rather than by theory. ---
examples: The idea has never been tested empirically.
Their claims are empirically supported by years of data.
Researchers set out to measure the effect empirically.
entries.position: end — after the verb; before its word with participles (empirically tested)

entries.meaning: All together, as a large group. ---
examples: The workers walked out en masse to protest the pay cuts.
Fans arrived en masse hours before the concert.
The board resigned en masse after the scandal.
entries.type: manner — all together as a group

entries.meaning: On the way to or from a place. ---
examples: We stopped for lunch en route to Denver.
The package is en route and should arrive Friday.
The ambulance is already en route.
entries.position: end — often followed by to or from

entries.meaning: In a way that gives someone hope or confidence. ---
examples: The coach smiled encouragingly at the nervous player.
"You're almost there," she said encouragingly.
Encouragingly, sales rose for the third month in a row.
entries.position: end — after the verb; front as a comment on the whole sentence

entries.meaning: In a way that makes people like someone, often in spite of a small flaw. ---
examples: He was endearingly awkward on their first date.
The puppy is endearingly clumsy.
Her notes are full of endearingly bad drawings.
entries.position: before its word — before an adjective (endearingly awkward)

entries.meaning: Without stopping, or seeming never to stop. ---
examples: My brother talks endlessly about football.
The debate went on endlessly.
I find the city endlessly fascinating.
entries.position: end — after the verb; before its word before an adjective

entries.meaning: In a way that lasts for a long time. ---
examples: The song has stayed enduringly popular for fifty years.
Her novels have proved enduringly influential.
It's one of the most enduringly successful shows on TV.
entries.position: before its word — before an adjective (enduringly popular)
entries.modifies: adjectives such as popular, influential, successful

entries.meaning: With a lot of energy and effort. ---
examples: The kids danced energetically to the music.
She campaigned energetically for the new park.
He scrubbed the pan energetically.
entries.position: end — after the verb or its object

entries.meaning: In a pleasant, charming way that holds your attention. ---
examples: The book is engagingly written and easy to follow.
She spoke engagingly about her years in Alaska.
He smiled engagingly and asked for one more chance.
entries.position: end — after the verb; before its word with participles (engagingly written)
entries.modifies: verbs of speaking and writing; participles and adjectives

entries.meaning: In a mysterious way that is hard to understand or explain. ---
examples: She smiled enigmatically and said nothing.
"You'll see," he replied enigmatically.
The note was enigmatically signed with a single initial.
entries.modifies: verbs such as smile, say, reply

entries.meaning: With great excitement and interest. ---
examples: The audience applauded enthusiastically.
She enthusiastically agreed to join the band.
Voters responded enthusiastically to the plan.

entries.meaning: To a degree that makes other people wish they had the same. ---
examples: She stays enviably calm under pressure.
At sixty, he's still enviably fit.
They live on an enviably quiet street.
entries.position: before its word — before an adjective
entries.contrast: Enviably describes something other people would like to have (enviably fit). Enviously describes the person who feels the envy (She looked at him enviously).

entries.meaning: In a way that shows you wish you had what someone else has. ---
examples: He looked enviously at his friend's new car.
The younger kids watched enviously from the sidelines.
"Must be nice," she said enviously.
entries.modifies: verbs such as look, watch, say

entries.meaning: Equally has 2 distinct senses.
examples: Both candidates are equally qualified.
Diet and exercise are equally important.
The two methods work equally well.
We split the bill equally.
The law should apply equally to everyone.

senses.head: To the same degree or extent
examples: Both candidates are equally qualified.
Diet and exercise are equally important.
The two methods work equally well.

senses.head: In equal parts, or in the same way for everyone
examples: We split the bill equally.
The law should apply equally to everyone.

entries.type: degree; also manner (split it equally) and linking (Equally, ...)
entries.position: before its word — before an adjective or adverb (equally good); end after a verb (share equally)
entries.contrast: Equally as (equally as good) is common in speech, but careful writers drop as: equally good, or just as good.

entries.meaning: Fairly, so that everyone gets a reasonable share. ---
examples: The money will be distributed equitably among the schools.
All employees must be treated equitably.
They worked out a way to divide the chores equitably.
entries.position: end — after the verb or its object
entries.modifies: verbs such as distribute, share, treat

entries.meaning: Therefore; used to introduce a logical result. ---
examples: He lied under oath; ergo, he can't be trusted.
The store was closed, ergo no milk for breakfast.
She's the boss, ergo she makes the rules.
entries.position: front — at the start of the result clause, usually after a comma or semicolon
entries.modifies: a clause that states a logical result
entries.contrast: It sounds bookish or mock-logical. In everyday speech say so, and in writing therefore.

entries.meaning: In a way that involves or suggests sexual desire. ---
examples: The film has an erotically charged atmosphere.
The poem is erotically suggestive without being explicit.
The two dancers moved erotically through a slow tango.
entries.position: before its word — before an adjective or participle (erotically charged); end after a verb

entries.meaning: In an irregular, unpredictable way. ---
examples: The car was swerving erratically across both lanes.
His heart had been beating erratically all night.
The old printer works erratically at best.

entries.meaning: Wrongly; by mistake. ---
examples: Several news outlets erroneously reported that he had died.
The charge was erroneously added to my bill.
The supplement is often erroneously described as harmless.
entries.position: mid — before the main verb or the past participle (erroneously reported)

entries.meaning: And other things of the same kind; and so on. ---
examples: Bring a towel, sunscreen, water, etc.
Pens, paper, folders, etc., are in the supply closet.
The fee covers food, drinks, music, etc.
entries.русский: и т. д., и так далее
entries.position: end — at the end of a list, after a comma
entries.form: abbreviation of Latin et cetera 'and the rest'; also written out as etcetera
entries.contrast: Never and etc. — et already means 'and'. Do not end a list with etc. after such as, e.g. or including, which already say the list is incomplete. Read aloud it is et cetera, with a t sound, not ek-cetera.

entries.meaning: Forever; also used to exaggerate how much or how long. ---
examples: I'll be eternally grateful for your help.
Many religions teach that the soul lives eternally.
He seems eternally optimistic, no matter what happens.
entries.position: before its word — before an adjective (eternally grateful); end after a verb

entries.meaning: In terms of a group's shared culture, origin or ancestry. ---
examples: Queens is one of the most ethnically diverse places in the country.
The neighborhood is ethnically mixed.
Ethnically, she's half Korean and half Mexican.
entries.position: before its word — before an adjective (ethnically diverse); front as a comment

entries.meaning: Using a mild or vague word in place of one that sounds harsh or unpleasant. ---
examples: The layoffs were euphemistically called "restructuring."
Prisons are sometimes euphemistically known as "correctional facilities."
He euphemistically described the crash as "a minor incident."
entries.position: mid — usually before called, known as or described as

entries.meaning: In a way that avoids giving a clear or direct answer. ---
examples: When asked about the money, he answered evasively.
"We'll see," she said evasively.
The senator responded evasively to every question about the deal.
entries.position: end — after a verb of speaking

entries.meaning: In spite of what was just said. ---
examples: The hotel was a little noisy. Even so, we enjoyed our stay.
It's an old car, but even so, it runs well.
I know it's risky; even so, I want to try.
entries.русский: и всё же, тем не менее

entries.meaning: Very; to a great degree, often about something small or delicate. ---
examples: The door opened ever so slightly.
She lifted the sleeping baby ever so gently.
Things are improving, ever so slowly.
entries.modifies: adjectives and adverbs, in American English mostly slightly, gently, slowly
entries.contrast: In American English it mostly stresses how small or gentle something is: ever so slightly, ever so gently. Thanks ever so and ever so nice sound British.

entries.meaning: In every way; just as much. ---
examples: The sequel is every bit as good as the original.
She was every bit as nervous as I was.
Moving to New York was every bit the adventure I'd hoped for.
entries.русский: ничуть не менее, во всех отношениях
entries.position: before its word — usually in every bit as … as
entries.modifies: adjectives and adverbs in as … as; a noun phrase (every bit a leader)

entries.meaning: Occasionally; not often and not regularly. ---
examples: Every now and then, we order pizza instead of cooking.
I still think about her every now and then.
He checks his phone every now and then during the meeting.

entries.meaning: Occasionally, at more or less regular intervals. ---
examples: Every so often, a train rumbles past the house.
Stir the soup every so often so it doesn't burn.
We meet up for coffee every so often.

entries.meaning: Every which way has 2 distinct senses.
examples: When the dog ran in, the chickens scattered every which way.
Kids were running every which way across the playground.
The books were piled on the shelves every which way.
Cars were parked every which way after the game.

senses.head: In all directions
examples: When the dog ran in, the chickens scattered every which way.
Kids were running every which way across the playground.

senses.head: In a messy, disorderly way
examples: The books were piled on the shelves every which way.
Cars were parked every which way after the game.

entries.type: direction — in all directions; also manner: in disorder
entries.contrast: Informal American.

entries.meaning: In or to every place; everywhere. ---
examples: I've looked everyplace for my keys.
There were people everyplace you turned.
You can't just leave your stuff everyplace.
entries.position: end — after the verb or its object
entries.contrast: An informal American word. In writing, and in most speech, use everywhere.

entries.meaning: In terms of evolution. ---
examples: Whales and hippos are evolutionarily close relatives.
The trait is evolutionarily ancient.
Evolutionarily speaking, fear kept our ancestors alive.
entries.position: before its word — before an adjective; front as a comment (Evolutionarily speaking)
entries.form: -ly from evolutionary, with y becoming i

entries.meaning: Too much; more than is reasonable or necessary. ---
examples: The meeting was excessively long.
He was fined for driving excessively fast.
Drinking excessively can damage your liver.
entries.position: before its word — before an adjective or adverb (excessively long); end after a verb (drink excessively)

entries.meaning: In a happy, eager way, full of energy and emotion. ---
examples: The kids talked excitedly about the trip.
She waved excitedly when she saw us.
Fans excitedly lined up outside the stadium.

entries.meaning: Extremely, to a degree that is painful or very hard to bear. ---
examples: The injury was excruciatingly painful.
The movie was excruciatingly slow.
Traffic moved excruciatingly slowly all the way home.
entries.position: before its word — before an adjective or adverb

entries.meaning: Completely and thoroughly, covering every part or detail. ---
examples: The drug was tested exhaustively before approval.
She researched the topic exhaustively.
The report exhaustively lists every known case.
entries.position: end — after the verb or its object
entries.modifies: verbs such as research, test, list
entries.contrast: Exhaustively is about thoroughness, not tiredness: the adjective for 'very tired' is exhausted, and 'in a tiring way' is exhaustingly.

entries.meaning: Far too much; used about prices and costs. ---
examples: The hotel is exorbitantly expensive.
Tickets were exorbitantly priced.
Rents in the area have risen exorbitantly.
entries.position: before its word — before an adjective or participle (exorbitantly priced); end after a verb
entries.modifies: adjectives and participles about price and cost

entries.meaning: Expansively has 2 distinct senses.
examples: After dinner he talked expansively about his plans.
She gestured expansively toward the view.
The courts have read the law expansively.
The term is now used much more expansively than it was.

senses.head: In a relaxed, open way, talking freely or making wide gestures
examples: After dinner he talked expansively about his plans.
She gestured expansively toward the view.

senses.head: Broadly, so as to cover a lot
examples: The courts have read the law expansively.
The term is now used much more expansively than it was.

entries.position: end — after the verb or its object
entries.modifies: verbs of talking, gesturing and interpreting

entries.meaning: In a way that shows you are waiting for something to happen. ---
examples: The dog looked up at me expectantly.
The audience waited expectantly for the band.
She paused expectantly, hoping someone would answer.
entries.modifies: verbs such as look, wait, pause

entries.meaning: Quickly and efficiently; without unnecessary delay. ---
examples: The court wants the case resolved as expeditiously as possible.
Your refund will be processed expeditiously.
The city moved expeditiously to repair the water main.
entries.position: end — also mid, before the main verb

entries.meaning: In a way that costs a lot of money. ---
examples: She was expensively dressed in a gray wool coat.
The apartment was expensively remodeled last year.
They live expensively for two people on a teacher's salary.
entries.position: mid or end — before a past participle (expensively dressed) or after the verb

entries.meaning: By means of experiments or as a trial. ---
examples: The theory has never been tested experimentally.
The drug is still being used experimentally in a few hospitals.
The school introduced the four-day week experimentally for one semester.

entries.meaning: With great skill. ---
examples: The chef expertly filleted the fish in under a minute.
The furniture is expertly crafted from solid oak.
She handled the angry customers expertly.
entries.position: mid or end — before a past participle (expertly made) or after the verb

entries.meaning: Clearly and directly, leaving no doubt. ---
examples: The contract explicitly says that pets are not allowed.
I told him explicitly not to touch the thermostat.
The law doesn't explicitly mention electric scooters.

entries.meaning: Suddenly and violently, like an explosion. ---
examples: The company grew explosively in its first two years.
The tank could react explosively if it overheats.
He laughed explosively and nearly spilled his coffee.

entries.meaning: Faster and faster, at an ever-increasing rate; by a very large amount. ---
examples: The number of users has grown exponentially since the launch.
Costs rise exponentially as you add more features.
The second exam was exponentially harder than the first.
entries.position: end — after the verb (grow exponentially); before its word in exponentially more

entries.meaning: In a way that clearly shows feelings or meaning. ---
examples: She plays the cello very expressively.
He talks expressively with his hands.
Try to read the poem more expressively this time.

entries.meaning: Expressly has 2 distinct senses.
examples: Smoking is expressly prohibited anywhere on campus.
The will expressly states that the house goes to her.
The app was designed expressly for people with poor eyesight.
She came to Chicago expressly to see the exhibit.

senses.head: Clearly and definitely, in words that leave no doubt
examples: Smoking is expressly prohibited anywhere on campus.
The will expressly states that the house goes to her.

senses.head: For one particular purpose only
examples: The app was designed expressly for people with poor eyesight.
She came to Chicago expressly to see the exhibit.

entries.position: mid — before the verb or past participle
entries.modifies: verbs, past participles and phrases of purpose (expressly for)

entries.meaning: In a very beautiful, delicate or refined way; also, intensely. ---
examples: The dress was exquisitely embroidered with silver thread.
The restaurant serves exquisitely prepared seafood.
The last few minutes of the game were exquisitely tense.
entries.position: before its word — exquisitely made, exquisitely painful

entries.meaning: Without preparation or notes. ---
examples: The senator lost her notes and spoke extemporaneously for twenty minutes.
Good debaters can argue extemporaneously on almost any topic.
The band played the final number extemporaneously.

entries.meaning: Over a large area or to a great extent; in detail. ---
examples: She has traveled extensively in South America.
The house was extensively damaged in the fire.
He has written extensively about the Civil War.
entries.position: end — also mid, before a past participle

entries.meaning: Externally has 2 distinct senses.
examples: This cream is to be applied externally only.
Externally, the car looks almost new.
The hard drive connects externally through a USB port.
The job was advertised both internally and externally.
The accounts are audited externally every year.

senses.head: On or from the outside of something, especially the body
examples: This cream is to be applied externally only.
Externally, the car looks almost new.
The hard drive connects externally through a USB port.

senses.head: By people or organizations outside a company or institution
examples: The job was advertised both internally and externally.
The accounts are audited externally every year.

entries.position: end — also mid, before a past participle

entries.meaning: Extra has 2 distinct senses.
examples: Be extra careful on the stairs — they're icy.
I'll have a coffee, extra hot, please.
She worked extra hard before the finals.
Delivery costs extra.
They charge extra for a room with a view.

senses.head: More than usually; especially
examples: Be extra careful on the stairs — they're icy.
I'll have a coffee, extra hot, please.
She worked extra hard before the finals.

senses.head: In addition to the usual amount or price
examples: Delivery costs extra.
They charge extra for a room with a view.

entries.position: before its word — extra careful; end in pay extra, charge extra
entries.modifies: adjectives and adverbs; verbs of paying and charging
entries.form: flat — the same form as the adjective extra
entries.contrast: An extra hour and extra cheese are the adjective, not this adverb. Before an adjective the adverb means 'more than usual': extra large is a size, extra careful is very careful — not 'too' careful.

entries.meaning: Extravagantly has 2 distinct senses.
examples: They lived extravagantly until the money ran out.
He spent extravagantly on cars and parties.
The ballroom was extravagantly decorated with gold and crystal.
Critics extravagantly praised her first novel.

senses.head: Spending more money than is sensible
examples: They lived extravagantly until the money ran out.
He spent extravagantly on cars and parties.

senses.head: In a showy or excessive way; far beyond what is usual
examples: The ballroom was extravagantly decorated with gold and crystal.
Critics extravagantly praised her first novel.

entries.position: end — also before its word (extravagantly praised)

entries.meaning: In a very happy, lively and energetic way. ---
examples: The fans cheered exuberantly when the final whistle blew.
The kids ran exuberantly into the waves.
She waved exuberantly from the other side of the street.

entries.meaning: In a way that shows great joy at a success or victory. ---
examples: "We did it!" she shouted exultantly.
The team lifted the trophy exultantly over their heads.
He grinned exultantly as the results came in.

entries.meaning: Extremely, to an almost unbelievable degree. ---
examples: He's a fabulously wealthy real estate developer.
The show was fabulously successful on Broadway.
The hotel has a fabulously expensive rooftop bar.

entries.meaning: Face-to-face has 2 distinct senses.
examples: We've talked on Zoom, but we've never met face-to-face.
Some things are better discussed face-to-face.
On the trail we came face-to-face with a black bear.
Working in the ER, she came face-to-face with the opioid crisis.

senses.head: In each other's physical presence, not by phone, email or video
examples: We've talked on Zoom, but we've never met face-to-face.
Some things are better discussed face-to-face.

senses.head: come face-to-face with: to meet or confront someone or something directly
examples: On the trail we came face-to-face with a black bear.
Working in the ER, she came face-to-face with the opioid crisis.

entries.contrast: Before a noun it is an adjective and always hyphenated: a face-to-face meeting. As an adverb you will see both meet face-to-face and meet face to face.

entries.meaning: Jokingly, often about something serious or at the wrong moment. ---
examples: "Maybe we should just move to Canada," he said facetiously.
I was speaking facetiously — I don't really want a third cat.
She facetiously suggested we hold the meeting at the beach.

entries.meaning: In terms of the facts; as regards what is true. ---
examples: The report is factually accurate but badly written.
His claim was factually incorrect.
The story is factually based, though the names have been changed.
entries.русский: с точки зрения фактов, по фактам
entries.type: viewpoint — with respect to the facts
entries.modifies: adjectives such as correct, accurate, wrong; verbs
entries.contrast: A false friend: Russian фактически means 'in fact, actually' — that is actually or in effect in English. Factually only means 'in terms of facts': The article is factually wrong.

entries.meaning: Faintly has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The kitchen smelled faintly of garlic.
He looked faintly embarrassed.
The idea seemed faintly ridiculous to me.
She smiled faintly but didn't say anything.
We could faintly hear music from next door.

senses.head: Slightly; a little
examples: The kitchen smelled faintly of garlic.
He looked faintly embarrassed.
The idea seemed faintly ridiculous to me.

senses.head: Weakly; so that it is hard to see or hear
examples: She smiled faintly but didn't say anything.
We could faintly hear music from next door.

entries.position: before its word — faintly amused; end after a verb (smiled faintly)

entries.meaning: Faithfully has 2 distinct senses.
examples: He served the company faithfully for thirty years.
She faithfully calls her mother every Sunday.
My grandfather faithfully watched every Cubs game.
The movie follows the book faithfully.
The old theater has been faithfully restored.

senses.head: Loyally and reliably, without stopping
examples: He served the company faithfully for thirty years.
She faithfully calls her mother every Sunday.
My grandfather faithfully watched every Cubs game.

senses.head: Accurately; exactly as the original
examples: The movie follows the book faithfully.
The old theater has been faithfully restored.

entries.position: end — also mid, before the verb
entries.contrast: Yours faithfully is a British way to end a formal letter; Americans write Sincerely or Sincerely yours.

entries.meaning: Wrongly; in a way that is not true. ---
examples: He spent ten years in prison after being falsely accused.
The website falsely claimed the product was made in the USA.
Many people falsely believe that lightning never strikes twice.
entries.position: mid or end — before a past participle (falsely accused) or after the verb

entries.meaning: Hesitantly, stopping and starting, without confidence. ---
examples: He spoke falteringly, looking down at his notes.
She walked falteringly across the room on her new crutches.
The engine started falteringly, then died.

entries.meaning: Familiarly has 2 distinct senses.
examples: Philadelphia is familiarly known as Philly.
The Federal National Mortgage Association, familiarly called Fannie Mae, buys home loans.
The new intern spoke to the CEO a little too familiarly.
He greeted everyone familiarly by their first names.

senses.head: Informally, in everyday use — mostly in familiarly known as
examples: Philadelphia is familiarly known as Philly.
The Federal National Mortgage Association, familiarly called Fannie Mae, buys home loans.

senses.head: In a very friendly, informal way, sometimes too much so
examples: The new intern spoke to the CEO a little too familiarly.
He greeted everyone familiarly by their first names.

entries.position: mid — before a past participle (familiarly known as); end after other verbs
entries.modifies: past participles such as known, called; verbs

entries.meaning: Famously has 2 distinct senses.
examples: Mark Twain famously said that the report of his death was an exaggeration.
The restaurant is famously difficult to get a table at.
He has written many books, most famously a series about a boy wizard.
The two dogs got along famously from day one.
The two families got along famously at the wedding.

senses.head: As is well known; in a way that many people know about
examples: Mark Twain famously said that the report of his death was an exaggeration.
The restaurant is famously difficult to get a table at.
He has written many books, most famously a series about a boy wizard.

senses.head: Very well — in get along famously
examples: The two dogs got along famously from day one.
The two families got along famously at the wedding.
