entries.position: mid — before the verb (famously said); end in get along famously
entries.comparison: more/most — most famously is common in the first sense

entries.meaning: With extreme, unreasonable enthusiasm or devotion. ---
examples: The team has a fanatically loyal following.
He trains fanatically, even on vacation.
She is fanatically neat about her desk.
entries.position: mid or end — before an adjective (fanatically loyal) or after the verb

entries.meaning: In an imaginative or unusual way, not based on reality. ---
examples: The cocktails on the menu are fancifully named.
The walls were fancifully painted with dragons and castles.
Some historians have fancifully suggested that he never existed.
entries.position: mid or end — before a past participle (fancifully named) or after the verb

entries.meaning: Fantastically has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The software is fantastically expensive.
She's a fantastically talented musician.
Their first album was fantastically successful.
The kids did fantastically at the swim meet.
The new system works fantastically.

senses.head: Extremely; to an unbelievable degree
examples: The software is fantastically expensive.
She's a fantastically talented musician.
Their first album was fantastically successful.

senses.head: Extremely well
examples: The kids did fantastically at the swim meet.
The new system works fantastically.

entries.position: before its word — fantastically rich; end in the manner sense

entries.meaning: By far; without any doubt. ---
examples: She is far and away the best player on the team.
This was far and away the hottest summer on record.
Rent is far and away our biggest expense.
entries.type: degree — by a very large margin
entries.position: before its word — before a superlative or the + noun
entries.modifies: superlatives and noun phrases with the

entries.meaning: Over a large area; in or from many places. ---
examples: People came from far and wide to hear him speak.
The news spread far and wide.
We searched far and wide for a good mechanic.

entries.meaning: In a way that follows current fashion. ---
examples: She's always fashionably dressed, even at the grocery store.
We arrived fashionably late, just after nine.
The loft is fashionably decorated with exposed brick and plants.
entries.position: mid or end — before a past participle or adjective (fashionably dressed, fashionably late)
entries.modifies: past participles, a few adjectives, and verbs

entries.meaning: With great, sometimes excessive care about detail, order or cleanliness. ---
examples: He fastidiously wiped down the counter after every use.
Her notes are fastidiously organized by date and topic.
The old car has been fastidiously maintained.

entries.meaning: Fatally has 2 distinct senses.
examples: Two people were fatally injured in the crash.
The officer was fatally shot while on duty.
The plan was fatally flawed from the start.
The campaign was fatally weakened by the scandal.

senses.head: In a way that causes death
examples: Two people were fatally injured in the crash.
The officer was fatally shot while on duty.

senses.head: In a way that leads to failure or disaster
examples: The plan was fatally flawed from the start.
The campaign was fatally weakened by the scandal.

entries.position: mid — before a past participle (fatally wounded, fatally flawed)

entries.meaning: Without any mistakes. ---
examples: The pianist played the whole concerto faultlessly.
Everything went faultlessly on the day of the wedding.
She answered every question faultlessly.

entries.meaning: With approval; in a way that shows or gives an advantage. ---
examples: Critics reviewed the play favorably.
Our prices compare favorably with those of our competitors.
The committee was favorably impressed by her proposal.
entries.position: end — also mid, before a past participle (favorably impressed)
entries.contrast: Favourably is the British spelling. Compare favorably with means 'be as good as or better than', not 'be compared in a friendly way'.

entries.meaning: In a frightened or anxious way. ---
examples: The child looked fearfully at the big dog.
"Is someone there?" she asked fearfully.
Investors are watching the markets fearfully.

entries.meaning: Without fear; bravely. ---
examples: The firefighters went fearlessly into the burning building.
She fearlessly spoke out against corruption.
Toddlers climb fearlessly, which is what scares their parents.
entries.position: end — also mid, before the verb

entries.meaning: By the federal government, or under federal law. ---
examples: The program is federally funded.
Minimum wage is set federally, but many states set a higher one.
Marijuana is legal in some states but still federally illegal.
entries.type: viewpoint — by or at the level of the national government

entries.meaning: Weakly; without strength, energy or conviction. ---
examples: The kitten meowed feebly from under the porch.
He feebly protested, but nobody listened.
"It was a joke," she said feebly.

entries.meaning: In a fierce, violent way; also, extremely. ---
examples: The dog barked ferociously at the mail carrier.
Both teams fought ferociously for the ball.
The tech industry is ferociously competitive.
entries.position: end — before its word as a degree adverb (ferociously competitive)

entries.meaning: With strong, sincere feeling. ---
examples: I fervently hope we never have to do that again.
She believes fervently in public education.
The crowd prayed fervently for rain.
entries.position: mid or end — before the verb (fervently hope) or after it

entries.meaning: Very quickly and with nervous excitement. ---
examples: Engineers worked feverishly to restore power.
He searched feverishly through his bag for his passport.
The staff were feverishly preparing for the inspection.
entries.position: end — also mid, before the verb

entries.meaning: Extremely — usually of something difficult or cleverly made. ---
examples: The Saturday crossword is fiendishly difficult.
It's a fiendishly clever plot.
The tax code is fiendishly complicated.

entries.meaning: Fiercely has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The two candidates argued fiercely about taxes.
The wind blew fiercely all night.
She is fiercely independent.
He's fiercely loyal to his friends.
The school is fiercely proud of its football team.

senses.head: In an angry, violent or aggressive way
examples: The two candidates argued fiercely about taxes.
The wind blew fiercely all night.

senses.head: Very strongly; intensely
examples: She is fiercely independent.
He's fiercely loyal to his friends.
The school is fiercely proud of its football team.

entries.position: end — before its word as a degree adverb (fiercely loyal)

entries.meaning: Not in the basic, literal meaning of the words; as a figure of speech. ---
examples: When I said he was a snake, I meant it figuratively.
The new mayor is, figuratively speaking, cleaning house.
The word heart is often used figuratively to mean courage.
entries.position: end — often in figuratively speaking; also front
entries.modifies: clauses; verbs such as use, mean, speak
entries.contrast: Figuratively is the opposite of literally. In casual American speech literally is often used where figuratively is meant (I literally died laughing); careful writers avoid this.

entries.meaning: Fine has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The old laptop still works fine.
Don't worry, you're doing fine.
Friday at two suits me fine.
Chop the onion fine before adding it to the pan.
Grind the coffee fine for espresso.

senses.head: Well; in a satisfactory way — informal
examples: The old laptop still works fine.
Don't worry, you're doing fine.
Friday at two suits me fine.

senses.head: Into very small pieces or very thin lines
examples: Chop the onion fine before adding it to the pan.
Grind the coffee fine for espresso.

entries.form: flat — the same form as the adjective fine
entries.contrast: In I'm fine and a fine day, fine is the adjective. The adverb in It works fine is informal but completely normal in American speech; formal writing uses well. Chop it fine and finely chopped mean the same thing.

entries.meaning: Finely has 2 distinct senses.
examples: Add two cloves of finely chopped garlic.
Top with finely grated Parmesan.
The engine is finely tuned for racing.
The two sides are finely balanced, so the vote could go either way.
It's a finely crafted novel.

senses.head: Into very small pieces or thin lines
examples: Add two cloves of finely chopped garlic.
Top with finely grated Parmesan.

senses.head: Precisely and delicately; in careful detail
examples: The engine is finely tuned for racing.
The two sides are finely balanced, so the vote could go either way.
It's a finely crafted novel.

entries.position: mid or end — usually before a past participle (finely chopped)

entries.meaning: Without changing your position or giving in. ---
examples: The union is standing firm on its demands.
Despite the pressure, the governor held firm.
Mortgage rates have held firm for three months.
entries.form: flat — the same form as the adjective firm
entries.contrast: The flat adverb lives almost only in stand firm and hold firm. Everywhere else use firmly: hold the rope firmly, I firmly believe.

entries.meaning: Firmly has 2 distinct senses.
examples: Hold the handle firmly and pull.
Make sure the car seat is firmly attached.
Press the lid down firmly until it clicks.
I firmly believe that everyone deserves a second chance.
"No more screens tonight," she said firmly.

senses.head: Tightly or securely, so that it does not move
examples: Hold the handle firmly and pull.
Make sure the car seat is firmly attached.
Press the lid down firmly until it clicks.

senses.head: Strongly and definitely, without changing your mind
examples: I firmly believe that everyone deserves a second chance.
"No more screens tonight," she said firmly.

entries.position: mid or end — before the verb (firmly believe) or after the verb and object

entries.meaning: In the most expensive and comfortable class, or by the fastest regular mail. ---
examples: The company flew her first class to Tokyo.
If I win the lottery, I'm traveling first class.
Send the letter first class so it gets there by Monday.
entries.type: manner — in the best class of travel or mail
entries.modifies: verbs of travel and sending: fly, travel, send
entries.contrast: As an adverb it takes no article or preposition: We flew first class. Before a noun it is an adjective, usually hyphenated: a first-class ticket, first-class service.

entries.meaning: Before anything else; as the first point. ---
examples: First of all, I want to thank everyone for coming.
First of all, you need a valid passport.
Well, first of all, I never said that.
entries.type: linking — the first point in a list or argument
entries.contrast: It opens a list of points or firmly states the most basic one. It does not mean at first (сначала, поначалу, when things later changed): At first I hated the job, not First of all I hated the job.

entries.meaning: Informal: first; to begin with. ---
examples: First off, let's make sure everyone has a copy.
First off, I'm not mad at you.
Okay, first off, what time does the store close?

entries.meaning: Directly, from your own experience rather than from other people. ---
examples: I saw firsthand how hard nurses work.
Students learn about farming firsthand by working on the farm.
She knows firsthand what it's like to be homeless.
entries.русский: из первых рук, на собственном опыте
entries.modifies: verbs such as see, learn, experience, know
entries.form: compound — first + hand; also spelled first-hand

entries.meaning: In terms of public money, taxes and budgets. ---
examples: She describes herself as fiscally conservative but socially liberal.
The mayor promised to be fiscally responsible with taxpayers' money.
The plan isn't fiscally sustainable in the long run.
entries.type: viewpoint — with respect to government or company money
entries.modifies: adjectives such as conservative, responsible, sound

entries.meaning: Irregularly, starting and stopping; not steadily. ---
examples: I slept fitfully on the overnight flight.
The fire burned fitfully in the wet wood.
The old generator ran fitfully all evening.

entries.meaning: In a way that is right or suitable for the situation. ---
examples: Fittingly, the award was presented in her hometown.
The dog is fittingly named Rocket.
The festival ended, fittingly, with a performance by local kids.
entries.type: stance — a comment that something is appropriate; also manner
entries.position: front — as a comment with a comma; mid before a past participle (fittingly named)

entries.meaning: Without moving the eyes; steadily. ---
examples: She stared fixedly at the phone, waiting for it to ring.
He looked fixedly out the window and didn't answer.
The cat watched the bird fixedly for ten minutes.

entries.meaning: In an obvious and shocking way — of breaking rules or laws. ---
examples: The company flagrantly violated safety regulations.
The referee ignored a flagrantly illegal hit.
He flagrantly disregarded the court's order.
entries.position: mid — before the verb, past participle or adjective (flagrantly violated, flagrantly illegal)

entries.meaning: In a bold, colorful way that attracts attention. ---
examples: The singer was flamboyantly dressed in pink feathers.
He gestures flamboyantly when he tells a story.
The house is flamboyantly decorated for Halloween every year.
entries.position: mid or end — before a past participle (flamboyantly dressed) or after the verb

entries.meaning: In a showy way meant to impress, often tastelessly. ---

The team plays flashily, but they don't win many games.
The casino is flashily lit with neon.
entries.position: mid or end — before a past participle (flashily dressed) or after the verb

entries.meaning: Flat out has 2 distinct senses.
examples: He flat out refused to sign the contract.
She told me flat out that she didn't trust me.
That's flat out wrong.
We've been working flat out to finish before the holidays.
The car was going flat out when it hit the wall.

senses.head: Directly and completely, without softening it
examples: He flat out refused to sign the contract.
She told me flat out that she didn't trust me.
That's flat out wrong.

senses.head: As fast or as hard as possible
examples: We've been working flat out to finish before the holidays.
The car was going flat out when it hit the wall.

entries.type: manner — bluntly; also degree: at full speed or effort
entries.position: mid or end — before the verb in the bluntly sense, after it in the full speed sense
entries.modifies: verbs; adjectives in the bluntly sense (flat out wrong)
entries.contrast: Informal and mainly American. Hyphenated before a noun it is an adjective meaning complete: a flat-out lie.

entries.meaning: Perfectly, without any mistakes or faults. ---
examples: The gymnast performed her routine flawlessly.
The software update installed flawlessly.
She speaks English flawlessly, with no accent at all.

entries.meaning: In a way that can change to suit different situations. ---
examples: Many employees now work flexibly from home.
The rules should be applied flexibly.
The funds can be used flexibly for any school project.

entries.meaning: Without the seriousness or respect a situation needs. ---
examples: "It's only money," he said flippantly.
She apologized for speaking so flippantly about the accident.
Don't answer the judge flippantly.

entries.meaning: In a way that playfully shows romantic interest. ---
examples: She smiled flirtatiously at him across the bar.
He winked flirtatiously and walked away.
They were chatting flirtatiously by the pool.

entries.meaning: Easily and without stopping — especially of speaking a language. ---
examples: She speaks Russian and Spanish fluently.
After a year abroad, he could read French fluently.
The more you practice, the more fluently you'll speak.

entries.meaning: Flush has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The new cabinets fit flush against the wall.
Mount the shelf flush with the edge of the counter.
The punch caught him flush on the jaw.
He hit the ball flush and it sailed over the fence.

senses.head: So as to be exactly level or in close contact with a surface
examples: The new cabinets fit flush against the wall.
Mount the shelf flush with the edge of the counter.

senses.head: Directly and squarely — of a hit or blow
examples: The punch caught him flush on the jaw.
He hit the ball flush and it sailed over the fence.

entries.modifies: verbs, usually with against, with or on
entries.form: flat — the same form as the adjective flush
entries.contrast: The adjective flush means 'having plenty of money' (flush with cash); the verb means to wash out with water (flush the toilet) or to turn red in the face. Neither is this adverb.

entries.meaning: With love and warm feelings. ---
examples: I remember my first teacher very fondly.
She smiled fondly at her grandchildren.
Locals still speak fondly of the old diner.
entries.position: mid or end — before the verb (fondly remember) or after it
entries.contrast: In older or literary English fondly imagine or fondly believe means 'foolishly and hopefully believe': He fondly imagined she would wait for him.

entries.meaning: In a silly or unwise way. ---
examples: I foolishly left my phone on the roof of the car.
Foolishly, we didn't check the weather before the hike.
He behaved foolishly at the party and regretted it.
entries.position: mid or end — also front as a comment (Foolishly, I said yes)

entries.meaning: For very little money. ---
examples: We bought the old farmhouse for a song.
The paintings went for a song at the estate sale.
He picked up a used guitar for a song.
entries.modifies: verbs of buying and selling: buy, sell, get, go

entries.meaning: For a period of time, usually not very long. ---
examples: Let's sit here for a while and rest.
I haven't seen him for a while.
She worked in Boston for a while before moving home.
entries.contrast: For a while is a length of time: I lived there for a while. In a while means after some time, soon (через некоторое время): I'll call you in a while.

entries.meaning: In every practical sense, even if not officially. ---
examples: For all intents and purposes, the deal is done.
The old factory is, for all intents and purposes, abandoned.
The election was over for all intents and purposes by ten o'clock.
entries.contrast: Often misheard and miswritten as for all intensive purposes. The British form is to all intents and purposes.

entries.meaning: In every way that matters in practice, even if not strictly or officially. ---
examples: For all practical purposes, the two phones are identical.
The town was, for all practical purposes, cut off by the flood.
Once they were up by twenty points, the game was over for all practical purposes.
entries.type: viewpoint — in practice, even if not strictly
entries.modifies: a whole clause; an adjective (for all practical purposes identical)

entries.meaning: Exactly; in every way, when something looks or seems like something else. ---
examples: From across the street, he looked for all the world like a movie star.
The recording sounds for all the world as if the band were in the room.
She stood there smiling, for all the world as though nothing had happened.
entries.position: before its word — before like, as if or as though
entries.modifies: like, as if or as though after look, sound, seem
entries.contrast: Do not confuse it with for the world in negatives: I wouldn't miss it for the world = ни за что на свете.

entries.meaning: Without any doubt. ---
examples: Nobody knows for certain what caused the fire.
I can't say for certain when he'll be back.
Do you know for certain that she's coming?
entries.contrast: Mostly after know, say or tell, often in negatives and questions: No one knows for certain. In everyday speech Americans more often say for sure.

entries.meaning: As hard or as fast as possible, as if to save one's life. ---
examples: The little boy held on to the railing for dear life.
We ran for dear life when the storm hit.
She clung to the edge of the raft for dear life.
entries.type: degree — as hard as possible, as if one's life depended on it
entries.modifies: verbs, usually hold on, cling, run

entries.meaning: Used to introduce something that shows what you mean. ---
examples: Many birds, for example penguins, cannot fly.
For example, you could take the train instead of driving.
Some jobs pay very little. Teaching assistants, for example, often earn less than $30,000.
entries.position: any position — front, mid between commas, or end
entries.modifies: a whole clause or a noun phrase
entries.contrast: For example is set off by commas and can move around the sentence; such as comes directly before the examples with no comma: cities such as Boston and Denver. Abbreviated e.g.

entries.meaning: Without having to pay. ---
examples: Kids under five get in for free.
I fixed his computer for free.
They were giving away T-shirts for free at the game.
entries.contrast: Free alone works too: Kids eat free. For free is informal but standard in American English. Do not confuse it with freely (свободно, открыто).

entries.meaning: Permanently; forever. ---
examples: She moved back to Ohio for good.
After the injury, he quit football for good.
I think the old diner has closed for good.
entries.contrast: For good means forever, not for a good reason or for the good of: He left for good = он уехал насовсем.

entries.meaning: As something extra, in addition to what is needed. ---
examples: He checked the locks twice, and once more for good measure.
Add a pinch of salt for good measure.
The waiter brought us a free dessert for good measure.
entries.type: manner — as an extra, beyond what is needed

entries.meaning: As an example. ---
examples: Some foods, for instance peanuts and eggs, often cause allergies.
For instance, you could start by walking to work.
Take my brother, for instance: he never learned to cook.
entries.modifies: a whole clause or a noun phrase

entries.meaning: Informal: permanently, to keep. ---
examples: You can have the book for keeps.
This time, she's leaving the city for keeps.
When he said he wanted to win, he was playing for keeps.
entries.contrast: Informal. Play for keeps comes from children's games where the winner keeps what is won, so it also means be completely serious.

entries.meaning: By any means at all; used only in negative sentences. ---
examples: You can't get a table there on a Saturday for love or money.
I couldn't find a taxi for love or money.
He wouldn't sell that truck for love or money.
entries.type: negative — used with a negative: by any means at all
entries.modifies: verbs in negative sentences, usually can't get or couldn't find

entries.meaning: For the present time, though this may change later. ---
examples: That's all for now.
Let's leave it here for now.
For now, the plan is to wait and see.
entries.contrast: For now means temporarily; by now means already, by this time (She should be home by now). Neither is the same as now.

entries.meaning: As one example of people who think or do something. ---
examples: I, for one, think it's a terrible idea.
Not everyone liked the movie. My wife, for one, walked out halfway through.
Plenty of people have doubts: the mayor, for one.
entries.type: focusing — singles out one example, often the speaker
entries.position: after its word — right after a noun or pronoun, between commas
entries.modifies: a noun or pronoun, usually the subject

entries.meaning: As a shorter form of a name. ---
examples: His name is Robert, but everyone calls him Bob for short.
The Federal Bureau of Investigation, or FBI for short, opened a case.
It's called the International Space Station, ISS for short.
entries.modifies: verbs of naming: call, be known as

entries.meaning: For sure has 2 distinct senses.
examples: I don't know for sure if the store is open.
We'll know for sure after the test results come back.
Nobody can say for sure who will win.
'Are you coming to the party?' 'For sure!'
That was for sure the best meal I've had all year.

senses.head: With certainty
examples: I don't know for sure if the store is open.
We'll know for sure after the test results come back.
Nobody can say for sure who will win.

senses.head: Informal: definitely; used to agree strongly
examples: 'Are you coming to the party?' 'For sure!'
That was for sure the best meal I've had all year.

entries.position: end — also alone as a reply
entries.modifies: verbs, especially know; a whole statement

entries.meaning: Used to say that what is true of one thing is also true of another. ---
examples: I don't trust him, or his brother for that matter.
She never calls her parents, or anyone else, for that matter.
Why would anyone, for that matter, want to live there?
entries.русский: если на то пошло, да и вообще
entries.type: linking — adds that the point applies to something else too
entries.modifies: a noun phrase or a whole clause

entries.meaning: Simply by asking for it, with no other effort or cost. ---
examples: The job is yours for the asking.
Free coffee is available for the asking at the front desk.
With his connections, a record deal was his for the asking.
entries.modifies: be or have: it's yours for the asking

entries.meaning: On the first occasion ever. ---
examples: I saw the ocean for the first time last summer.
For the first time in years, she took a real vacation.
He's cooking dinner for the first time, so be kind.
entries.contrast: For the first time = the first occasion ever; at first = at the beginning, before a change; first = before anything else. Russian впервые is only the first of these.

entries.meaning: Now, for a short time, though things may change. ---
examples: For the moment, we're staying with my parents.
The rain has stopped for the moment.
Let's leave that question aside for the moment.
entries.type: time — for now, though it may change

entries.meaning: Mostly; in most cases. ---
examples: For the most part, the students behaved well.
The reviews were, for the most part, positive.
I agree with you for the most part.

entries.meaning: For now, until something changes. ---
examples: For the time being, the office is closed.
You can use my old laptop for the time being.
We're renting an apartment for the time being.

entries.meaning: Strongly and with conviction; with energy. ---
examples: She argued forcefully for a new approach.
The president spoke forcefully about the need for change.
He pushed the door forcefully, and it finally opened.
entries.modifies: verbs, especially of speaking and arguing
entries.contrast: Forcefully is about strength and conviction: She argued forcefully. Forcibly is about physical force against someone's will: He was forcibly removed.

entries.meaning: By using physical force, against someone's will. ---
examples: Two protesters were forcibly removed from the meeting.
Thousands of families were forcibly relocated.
The police had to open the door forcibly.
entries.position: mid or end — before a past participle (forcibly removed) or after the verb
entries.contrast: Forcibly means 'using physical force'; forcefully means 'strongly, with conviction': forcibly evicted but forcefully argued.

entries.meaning: first and foremost: most importantly; above all. ---
examples: First and foremost, I'm a mother.
The job is, first and foremost, about keeping people safe.
We need, first and foremost, a clear budget.
entries.position: front — as first and foremost, usually with a comma
entries.contrast: In the world's foremost expert (leading, most important) foremost is an adjective, not this adverb.

entries.meaning: In a sad, lonely and hopeless way. ---
examples: The puppy looked up at us forlornly from the shelter cage.
An old bicycle leaned forlornly against the fence.
He waited forlornly by the phone.

entries.meaning: Formally has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The company formally announced the merger on Monday.
She was formally charged with fraud.
We haven't been formally introduced.
Guests are asked to dress formally.
He always writes very formally, even in text messages.

senses.head: Officially, following the proper rules or procedure
examples: The company formally announced the merger on Monday.
She was formally charged with fraud.
We haven't been formally introduced.

senses.head: In a formal style, not casually
examples: Guests are asked to dress formally.
He always writes very formally, even in text messages.

entries.position: mid or end — before the verb (formally announced) or after it (dress formally)
entries.contrast: A false friend: Russian формально often means 'only on paper, nominally' — that is technically or nominally in English. Formally means 'officially' or 'in a formal style': He was formally charged is a real, official charge.

entries.meaning: Impressively, to a degree that makes someone or something hard to deal with or beat. ---
examples: She's a formidably intelligent trial lawyer.
The team looks formidably strong this season.
The bar exam is formidably difficult.

entries.meaning: Forth has 4 distinct senses.
examples: He paced back and forth in the waiting room.
We emailed back and forth about the details all week.
Bring a towel, sunscreen, a hat, and so forth.
The fee covers books, lab equipment and so forth.
The explorers set forth at dawn.
The report sets forth three possible solutions.
A spring of cold water gushed forth from the rock.
From that day forth, she never missed a practice.
From this moment forth, you are free.

senses.head: back and forth: from one place or side to the other, again and again
examples: He paced back and forth in the waiting room.
We emailed back and forth about the details all week.

senses.head: and so forth: and other similar things
examples: Bring a towel, sunscreen, a hat, and so forth.
The fee covers books, lab equipment and so forth.

senses.head: Forward, out or away — formal, with verbs such as set, go, come, bring
examples: The explorers set forth at dawn.
The report sets forth three possible solutions.
A spring of cold water gushed forth from the rock.

senses.head: from that day forth, from now forth: from that time on — formal
examples: From that day forth, she never missed a practice.
From this moment forth, you are free.

entries.modifies: verbs of movement and a few fixed phrases
entries.contrast: Forth and fourth sound exactly the same. Outside fixed phrases (back and forth, and so forth, set forth) everyday English uses forward or out.

entries.meaning: Directly and honestly, without hiding anything. ---
examples: The coach spoke forthrightly about the team's mistakes.
She answered the reporters' questions forthrightly.
The senator addressed the scandal more forthrightly than anyone expected.

entries.meaning: Immediately — formal and legal. ---
examples: The contract may be terminated forthwith if either party breaks these terms.
The judge ordered that the prisoner be released forthwith.
The resignation takes effect forthwith.

entries.meaning: By a lucky chance. ---
examples: Fortuitously, a doctor was sitting in the next row.
The meeting was fortuitously timed, just before the vote.
We fortuitously found a parking spot right in front.
entries.position: front — as a comment with a comma; also mid
entries.contrast: Strictly, fortuitously means 'by chance', lucky or not. Most Americans now use it to mean 'luckily', and some careful writers object to that.

entries.meaning: By four times as much. ---
examples: The price of eggs has increased fourfold in a year.
Online sales grew fourfold during the pandemic.
The risk rises almost fourfold for smokers.
entries.modifies: verbs such as increase, grow, rise

entries.meaning: In a hurried, desperate way, out of fear or worry. ---
examples: She searched frantically for her keys.
Parents were frantically calling the school.
The man waved frantically for help.
entries.position: end — also mid, before the verb

entries.meaning: By deceiving people, illegally, usually to get money. ---
examples: He fraudulently claimed unemployment benefits for two years.
The loans were obtained fraudulently.
Her signature was fraudulently used on the documents.

entries.meaning: To a strange or unnaturally extreme degree — informal. ---
examples: The new center is freakishly tall — almost seven foot four.
It was freakishly warm for February.
My little brother is freakishly good at math.

entries.meaning: Without any cost. ---
examples: Delivery is free of charge on orders over $50.
The museum is open to the public free of charge.
They repaired the phone free of charge because it was under warranty.
entries.contrast: More formal than for free; common in notices and ads. Charge here means price.

entries.meaning: In a fast, energetic and disorganized way. ---
examples: Waiters rushed frenetically between the tables.
The band played frenetically until midnight.
Reporters were typing frenetically as the results came in.

entries.meaning: Fresh has 2 distinct senses.
examples: She's fresh out of law school.
The bread is fresh from the oven.
He came to the meeting fresh off a red-eye flight.
Sorry, we're fresh out of blueberry muffins.
I'm fresh out of ideas — any suggestions?

senses.head: Very recently; just
examples: She's fresh out of law school.
The bread is fresh from the oven.
He came to the meeting fresh off a red-eye flight.

senses.head: fresh out of: having just sold or used up the last of something — informal
examples: Sorry, we're fresh out of blueberry muffins.
I'm fresh out of ideas — any suggestions?

entries.position: before its word — before out of, from, and a past participle
entries.modifies: prepositional phrases (fresh from, fresh out of) and past participles
entries.form: flat — the same form as the adjective fresh
entries.contrast: In fresh bread and fresh air, fresh is the adjective. Before a participle the flat adverb is informal and usually hyphenated (fresh-baked, fresh-squeezed); freshly baked is the neutral form.

entries.meaning: Recently — before a past participle. ---
examples: The house smelled of freshly baked bread.
I'd like a glass of freshly squeezed orange juice.
Watch out — the bench is freshly painted.

entries.meaning: In a worried, restless or irritable way. ---
examples: The baby cried fretfully all night.
"What if we miss the flight?" she asked fretfully.
He paced fretfully outside the operating room.

entries.meaning: In a way that causes fear; alarmingly. ---
examples: The storm moved in frighteningly fast.
It's frighteningly easy to steal someone's identity online.
The water level rose frighteningly close to the top of the levee.

entries.meaning: In a silly, unserious way; wastefully. ---
examples: He spent his first paycheck frivolously.
The court fines people who file lawsuits frivolously.
She was criticized for talking frivolously about a serious issue.

entries.meaning: Over the whole body; completely. ---
examples: The kids came home covered in mud from head to toe.
She was dressed in black from head to toe.
I was shaking from head to toe.
entries.type: degree — completely, all over the body
entries.modifies: verbs and adjectives describing the body or clothes

entries.meaning: Starting now and continuing into the future. ---
examples: From now on, I'm walking to work.
From now on, all requests go through Maria.
Things will be different from now on.
entries.contrast: The on is required: ✗ from now I will sounds unfinished, and ✗ since now is not English. For a date, use starting or from … on: starting Monday, from Monday on.

entries.meaning: From the very beginning, without using anything already done. ---
examples: The files were lost, so we had to start from scratch.
She built the business from scratch.
This cake is made from scratch, not from a box.
entries.type: manner — from the very beginning, with nothing prepared
entries.modifies: verbs, especially start, build, make, bake
entries.contrast: In cooking it means from basic ingredients, not from a mix: She bakes her bread from scratch.

entries.meaning: Through the whole of something, from beginning to end. ---
examples: The movie was exciting from start to finish.
The project took six months from start to finish.
She led the race from start to finish.

entries.meaning: Sincerely, expressing real feelings. ---
examples: His speech at the wedding came from the heart.
Just speak from the heart and you'll be fine.
I mean this from the heart: thank you.

entries.meaning: Occasionally; sometimes. ---
examples: We still see each other from time to time.
From time to time, the power goes out in our neighborhood.
Check the oil from time to time.

entries.meaning: In a cold, unfriendly way. ---
examples: "That's none of your business," she replied frostily.
The proposal was received frostily by the board.
He nodded frostily and left the room.

entries.meaning: Carefully, spending as little money as possible. ---
examples: They lived frugally and paid off the house in ten years.
My grandparents ate frugally but never went hungry.
If we travel frugally, we can stay a whole month.

entries.meaning: In a way that produces good or useful results. ---
examples: The two labs have worked together fruitfully for years.
Your time could be spent more fruitfully on the second chapter.
The idea could fruitfully be applied to other cities.

entries.meaning: Without success; with no result. ---
examples: We searched fruitlessly for a gas station.
He spent months fruitlessly trying to get a refund.
The two sides negotiated fruitlessly until dawn.

entries.meaning: For the whole of a normal working or study week. ---
examples: She works full-time and takes night classes.
He went back to work full-time after the baby turned one.
Most students here study full-time.
entries.русский: на полную ставку, полный рабочий день
entries.type: duration — for a whole normal working week
entries.modifies: verbs such as work, study, teach
entries.contrast: Before a noun it is always hyphenated: a full-time job. As an adverb you will see both work full-time and work full time. The opposite is part-time.

entries.meaning: Functionally has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The two phones are functionally identical.
The old building is functionally obsolete.
Millions of adults are functionally illiterate.
Without a budget, the agency is functionally dead.

senses.head: In terms of how something works or what it does
examples: The two phones are functionally identical.
The old building is functionally obsolete.

senses.head: For all practical purposes; in effect
examples: Millions of adults are functionally illiterate.
Without a budget, the agency is functionally dead.

entries.position: before its word — functionally identical, functionally illiterate

entries.meaning: Fundamentally has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The internet fundamentally changed the way we shop.
Their approaches are fundamentally different.
I fundamentally disagree with that decision.
Fundamentally, he's a good person who made a bad choice.
The problem is fundamentally about money.

senses.head: In a basic and very important way; completely
examples: The internet fundamentally changed the way we shop.
Their approaches are fundamentally different.
I fundamentally disagree with that decision.

senses.head: At the most basic level; essentially
examples: Fundamentally, he's a good person who made a bad choice.
The problem is fundamentally about money.

entries.русский: в корне, коренным образом; по сути
entries.position: before its word — fundamentally different; front with a comma in the second sense

entries.meaning: funnily enough: strangely or surprisingly. ---
examples: Funnily enough, I was just thinking about you.
Funnily enough, the cheaper hotel was nicer.
We grew up on the same street, funnily enough.
entries.position: front — as funnily enough, with a comma
entries.contrast: Funnily enough means 'strangely', not 'humorously'. In casual American speech funny enough is also common.

entries.meaning: Furiously has 2 distinct senses.
examples: "Get out of my office!" he shouted furiously.
She reacted furiously when she saw the bill.
He was typing furiously to meet the deadline.
The kids pedaled furiously up the hill.
The crew worked furiously to put out the fire.

senses.head: In a very angry way
examples: "Get out of my office!" he shouted furiously.
She reacted furiously when she saw the bill.

senses.head: With great energy, speed or effort
examples: He was typing furiously to meet the deadline.
The kids pedaled furiously up the hill.
The crew worked furiously to put out the fire.

entries.meaning: Secretly and nervously, trying not to be noticed. ---
examples: He glanced furtively at his phone during the meeting.
She furtively slipped the note into his pocket.
Two teenagers were smoking furtively behind the gym.

entries.meaning: Fussily has 2 distinct senses.
examples: He fussily straightened every fork on the table.
She rearranged the pillows fussily before the guests arrived.
The living room was fussily decorated with lace and china dolls.
The menu is fussily written, with three adjectives for every dish.

senses.head: With too much attention to small, unimportant details
examples: He fussily straightened every fork on the table.
She rearranged the pillows fussily before the guests arrived.

senses.head: With too much decoration or detail
examples: The living room was fussily decorated with lace and china dolls.
The menu is fussily written, with three adjectives for every dish.

entries.position: mid or end — before a past participle (fussily decorated) or after the verb

entries.meaning: Without any chance of success; in vain.
examples: He tried futilely to start the car in the freezing cold.
She searched futilely for her ring in the sand.
Neighbors futilely argued that the park should be saved.
